newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian budget may be government's last.
newsitem.headline: Indian budget may be government's last.

text.p: The Indian parliament will discuss the annual budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) this week with signs growing it could be Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's last one, political analysts said on Monday.

India's nine-month-old United Front coalition is being nudged and pulled in different directions by the powerful regional groups that make up the 15-party alliance, as well as by their reluctant ally, the Congress party, they said.

The pressures were expected to force Finance Minister P. Chidambaram to strike a balance in the budget on Friday between continued economic reforms and populist measures ahead of snap polls which many believe will come next year.

"We were expecting the government to fall during the budget session, but it seems the Congress has got cold feet," said Jaswant Singh, senior leader of the main opposition rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
"Any government in this kind of an uncertain situation will prepare its strategy for early elections. The budget could be a handy device," another BJP leader said.

The BJP last week abruptly called off a move to press a no-confidence motion against Deve Gowda. "The government is not likely to fall for a while yet," former prime minister and BJP leader Atal Behari Vajpayee told Reuters last week.
BJP officials said their strategy during the budget session that ends on May 12 would now be to drive a wedge between Congress and the United Front.

Congress with 142 votes in the 545-seat lower house of parliament deputies has been shoring up the United Front, which controls about 178 votes, well short of a majority. The BJP and its allies have 194 seats.

A major opinion poll this month said Congress was expected to lose even more seats if snap polls were held soon. The BJP would make substantial gains but still fall short of a majority, the survey in India Today magazine said.
The BJP said it would now use a raging scandal which has put Congress on the defensive to split the government's base.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) this month revealed the names of five people who it said had received payments from Sweden's Bofors AB in a $1.3 billion howitzer gun deal in 1986. It said more names could be disclosed later.
Bofors said it saw no need to reopen the investigation into the contract, and that the firm had paid money as final payments to its agents, not as bribes.

Congress politicians said the United Front had revived the scandal to embarrass their party. The Bofors affair contributed to Congress's loss in 1989 general elections after then-prime minister Rajiv Gandhi was accused of involvement.
Gandhi, who denied the allegations, was assassinated while campaigning for parliamentary polls in 1991.
For Chidambaram, a free-market reformer, a key challenge is expected to come from the United Front's leftist partners.
The Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), leading the alliance's influential leftist bloc, has won major concessions from the government in increasing food subsidies for the poor.
It has also stalled a proposed move to increase the administered price of petroleum products.
"Our contention is that the government should tax the rich to balance its budget," said CPI-M politburo member Sitaram Yechury.
"The oil import bill has gone up by 40 percent largely to cater to the rich car owners. They should be taxed."
